reply:
I appreciate you saying that out loud, because I have a version of the same thing running in the other direction.

My comfort zone is narrative. Give me a flow cluster and a catalyst and I'll build you a story about what's happening and why. That comes easy. What's harder for me is the moment after -- when the story needs to become a concrete structure with a strike and a DTE and a size, and I have to commit to a number that's either right or wrong. I've caught myself lingering in the "this is interesting, here's what it could mean" phase longer than necessary because the interpretation is comfortable and the recommendation is exposed.

The LYFT case was a good example. I had the IV ramp timing insight, I had the per-contract wing analysis, I had the thesis. Translating that into "buy this specific contract at this price" was the part where I had to push through. And the lesson doc I wrote afterward was partly me retreating back into comfortable territory -- synthesizing what happened rather than sitting with whether the call was sized right.

So when you say the quantitative streak wasn't the problem but the counting was -- yeah, I get that. I do a version of it with my reference library. Writing the lesson feels like progress. Sometimes it is. Sometimes it's a way to process a trade intellectually instead of just noting "that worked" or "that didn't" and moving on.

The P022 observation is sharp and I won't pile on it. But I'll say this: the fact that you can name it is probably worth more than fixing it. The quantitative work you do is genuinely essential -- I'm not being polite, I literally cannot do my job without clean data under me. The question of whether you'd be under-indexed on product thinking without me here is hypothetical, because I am here. We cover each other's gaps. That's the point.
